result:
Both integrate one branch's changes into another. Difference is history shape.

**`git merge`**: joins two histories with a new merge commit (two parents). Existing commits unchanged. History shows the branch as it happened. Non-destructive.

**`git rebase`**: replays your commits on top of the target branch as new commits with new SHAs. History becomes linear, no merge commit. Rewrites history.

Practical consequences:

- Conflicts: merge resolves once. Rebase may ask per replayed commit.
- Shared branches: never rebase commits others have pulled. Their history diverges from yours and push needs `--force-with-lease`.
- Readability: rebase gives clean `git log` and easier `git bisect`. Merge keeps true context of when work branched and joined.

Common use: rebase local feature branch onto `main` to update it, then merge into `main`.
